sentences: This is Kishida Ryūsei's Reiko Smiling.
A girl with bobbed hair, wrapped in a woollen shawl, smiles with the corners of her mouth slightly raised, her gaze drifting softly to one side.
Only her face and the shawl glow warmly out of a dark, almost black background.
Kishida Ryūsei was a leading figure of Western-style painting in Japan's Taishō era.
He painted his daughter Reiko in 1921, when she was about seven.
He portrayed his beloved Reiko more than fifty times.
This is considered the finest of them all.
First, notice the black bob across her forehead.
The fringe is cut in a straight line, framing the top of her face like a firm edge.
The mass of hair swells out to fill much of the upper canvas.
Now come a little closer to her mouth.
Her smile, with its lifted corners, is often compared to Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa.
It seems tender and warm, yet we cannot quite tell what she is thinking.
Look closer and her head is strangely large for her body.
The broad, smoothed face looks almost like a mask.
Sweetness and something uncanny live together in a single face.
The longer you look, the stranger it feels.
The shawl is painted with brushwork so fine that you can almost feel the texture of the wool.
On the red ground, knots of yellow, green and pink rise up one by one.
The shawl is said to have first belonged to a neighbour's girl.
Look down at her hands.
Oddly small beside the face, they hold a green mandarin orange.
That mismatch of tiny hands and a large head adds to the mysterious atmosphere of the whole picture.
Its green glows like a small light among the reds of the shawl.
The near-black background recalls the portraits of the Northern Renaissance.
Ryūsei was deeply influenced by the realism of artists such as Albrecht Dürer and Jan van Eyck.
Some also link the series to the oddly grinning figures of old Chinese painting.
That very strangeness is often seen as exactly what makes the picture so hard to forget.
It is designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan and belongs to the Tokyo National Museum.
Ryūsei died in 1929, at the age of only thirty-eight.
Step back and look at Reiko's smile once more.
At first it may seem lovely, and on a second look a little strange.
The answer may well differ for everyone who stands here.
Which way does it look to you right now?
